data.content_ref: inline:The claim purports to defend Popper's preference for 'better-corroborated' theories, but the mechanism silently substitutes a different criterion: empirical content among unfalsified theories. The mechanism states the preference is 'not based on the probability of truth ... but on the severity of tests passed, which indicates high informational content,' then operationalizes selection as 'choosing the theory with highest empirical content that has not yet been falsified.' This conflates corroboration (a historical measure of how severely a theory has been tested and survived) with empirical content (a logical measure of how much a theory rules out). Two unfalsified theories can have identical empirical content yet differ in corroboration because one has passed more severe tests. By collapsing corroboration into 'informational content + not-yet-falsified,' the mechanism defends only the preference for informative surviving conjectures, not the preference for better-corroborated theories as Popper actually uses the term. Thus the defense is a bait-and-switch: it defends a weaker, content-based rule while claiming to defend the corroboration-based rule that is the target of the induction objection. The countercondition about Tichý/Miller further exposes the gap—if 'best-tested' cannot be coherently defined as 'closest to truth,' then the mechanism's equation of 'severity of tests passed' with 'high informational content' provides no account of why the *better-corroborated* (as opposed to merely more informative) theory should be preferred at all.
